characters: Antwi: a 12-year-old boy in a white shirt and brown shorts, holding a ruler.
Nyarko: his friend, 12, in a cap, with a notebook of numbers.
Madam Sowah: their teacher, in a floral dress, with a pointer.
Stonehenge: a ring of huge standing grey stones with flat stones across the tops, on green grassland.
Ancient builders: people in simple clothes and furs pulling a huge stone on logs with ropes.

narrationPlan.voice: Thoughtful storyteller voice; Madam Sowah is patient and wry
narrationPlan.pace: Steady and thoughtful, with awe at the stones (about 125 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: Slow drums and low strings with a hopeful theme, like footsteps pulling together (placeholder)
culturalNotes: Stonehenge is in England. Ghana has its own ancient and heritage sites, such as the Asante traditional buildings, the Larabanga Mosque and the forts and castles of the coast; pupils can compare them.
Teamwork and community building, such as “nnoboa” (working together on farms), are Ghanaian values; the story links them without claiming the builders had the same traditions.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?

Check the Altar Stone facts (likely northeast Scotland, at least 700 km, about six tonnes, 2024 study) against the UCL or Aberystwyth press release; the “Accra to Tamale” comparison needs a distance check.
The sarsen source (about 25 km away) and the sledge-and-log theory are drawn from general knowledge and need a named source before publication.
Confirm “nnoboa” is spelt and described correctly.

teacherGuide.overview: A partly solved mystery. Scientists have traced where stones came from, but nobody knows exactly how they were moved or what Stonehenge was for.
learningGoals: Describe how scientists trace the origin of a stone.
Explain what is known and unknown about Stonehenge.
beforeReading: Ask: how do people move something very heavy without machines?
whileReading: At page 5, check the Accra-to-Tamale comparison on a map.
afterReading: Try moving a heavy box with logs (rollers) and a rope, safely, as a team.
Compare Stonehenge with a Ghanaian heritage site.
discussion: What teamwork would it take to move a six-tonne stone?
Why might people build something so big?
reflection: What would you build with your community?

mathsExtension.task: If the Altar Stone travelled 700 km and a walking team covers 10 km a day, how many days would that take?
Stonehenge began about 5,000 years ago. If it is now 2026, about which year was that?

support: Provide a map with the sources of the stones.
stretch: Plan how a team of 200 people might pull a stone and what each group would do.

culturalNotes: Stonehenge is in England. Ghana has its own ancient and heritage sites, such as the Asante traditional buildings, the Larabanga Mosque and the forts and castles of the coast; pupils can compare them.
Teamwork and community building, such as “nnoboa” (working together on farms), are Ghanaian values; the story links them without claiming the builders had the same traditions.
localiseThis: Visit or discuss a local heritage site.
Do not climb or damage monuments; explain why heritage sites need protection.

whatWeKnow: Stonehenge was begun about 5,000 years ago.
The Altar Stone likely came from northeast Scotland, at least 700 km away.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: Exactly how the stones were moved.

factCheck.claim: The Altar Stone likely came from northeast Scotland (the Orcadian Basin), at least 700 km away; it weighs about six tonnes; Stonehenge construction began about 5,000 years ago.
factCheck.explanation: From an Aberystwyth University news release on the 2024 study.
factCheck.reference: Aberystwyth University, “Stonehenge Altar Stone came from Scotland, not Wales” (Aug 2024); the UCL page could not be opened in this session.

factCheck.claim: Sarsen stones came from about 25 km away; sledge-and-roller transport is a theory; purposes such as ceremony, calendar, burial or unity are debated.
factCheck.explanation: From memory and search headlines; not verified from a fetched page in this session.

pronunciation.guidance: Ghanaians often say "uh-KRAH" (stress on the second syllable).
